name: Vegan diet
lead: A vegan diet excludes all animal-derived foods, including meat, fish, dairy, eggs and honey, and is built around vegetables, fruit, legumes, grains, nuts and seeds. The word "vegan" dates to November 1944, when Donald Watson and others founded The Vegan Society in Leicester, England.[11][15][16] People in appearance communities discuss it as a route to a leaner physique, clearer-looking skin and, in some threads, lighter eye colour, and as a diet that bodybuilders either adapt to or avoid.[12][13][14]

The mechanism most often cited for a looks benefit is body composition. Randomised trials of low-fat vegan diets report weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity in overweight adults and people with type 2 diabetes, and a meta-analysis of trials found weight reduction on vegetarian diets, which is the chain from diet to leanness that proponents describe.[5][8][10][24] Claims about skin, hair and eye colour come from personal reports; trials of vegan diets measure weight, blood lipids and blood sugar rather than appearance.

Position statements from dietetic organisations describe well-planned vegan diets as suitable at all life stages, while reviews of dietary intake highlight vitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium, iodine, zinc and omega-3 as nutrients needing attention, and note lower average protein intake than in omnivorous diets.[7][11][17] Vegan diets are also discussed in sport, where a 2023 review concluded athletes can follow them with careful planning.[25]

chain: Plant-only eating, typically higher in fibre and lower in saturated fat
Weight loss and lower body fat reported in trials
Leaner physique; skin and hair effects reported anecdotally
angle.text: People use vegan eating to lose fat and reach a leaner look, and some report clearer skin. Trials document weight and cardiometabolic changes; appearance outcomes such as skin or hair have not been measured directly.

infobox: Plant-based diet; excludes all animal products[11]

paras: Veganism is both a diet and, for many followers, an ethical stance. Ethical vegans avoid animal products in clothing, entertainment and medicine as well as food, dietary vegans restrict food only, and environmental vegans are motivated by the ecological impact of animal farming.[11] The Vegan Society's current definition frames veganism as a way of living that seeks to exclude animal exploitation and cruelty, and it also covers diet.[16]

Within the diet, wide variation exists. A whole-food plant-based diet emphasises vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and seeds, and the term is attributed to the biochemist T. Colin Campbell, whose co-authored book The China Study appeared in 2005.[17] Low-fat vegan diets, used in several of the clinical trials below, restrict added oils and fatty plant foods. Raw veganism limits intake to uncooked plant foods, typically not heated above about 40 to 49 degrees Celsius, and includes fruitarian and sprouted-food subgroups.[19] Processed vegan convenience foods and meat substitutes are also part of many people's vegan eating, and a 2021 comment cited on Wikipedia raised concern that heavy reliance on them could lower diet quality.[17]

sections.h: How people use it to improve their looks
paras: Leanness is the clearest route. Trials in overweight adults and in people with type 2 diabetes report weight loss on low-fat vegan diets, and the diet's higher fibre and lower energy density are the explanations usually offered by researchers and proponents.[8][10][24][17] Wikipedia summarises a 2022 review finding about 4 kg of weight reduction on vegan diets lasting 12 weeks or longer.[17]

Skin is the second theme. Proponents describe clearer or brighter skin after dropping dairy or eating more produce. These accounts are anecdotal and no trial has measured skin appearance on a vegan diet. A related, well-documented effect is carotenoderma: eating large amounts of carotenoid-rich plant foods can give skin a yellow-orange tint, which is harmless and fades over weeks to months after intake falls, and is most visible in light-skinned people.[21]

Physique building is the third. Vegan bodybuilders and strength athletes exist, and the 2018 documentary The Game Changers presented several of them.[20] A 2023 review of vegan athletes concluded the evidence does not show that a vegan diet improves performance, adaptation or recovery, but also that athletes can follow one without detriment if protein and key micronutrients are planned for.[25] A 2023 meta-analysis summarised on Wikipedia found no effect of plant-based diets on strength.[17]

Vegetarian traditions are old, but the vegan diet as a named practice began in England. Donald Watson (1910-2005), a woodwork teacher who had been a vegetarian since age 14, left the Leicester Vegetarian Society with a small group that did not accept dairy, and in November 1944 they founded The Vegan Society and its newsletter, The Vegan News.[15][16] Wikipedia credits Watson and Dorothy Morgan, whom he married in 1946, with coining the word from the first three and last two letters of "vegetarian".[11][15] The first president was elected in 1946, the Vegan Trademark took effect in 1990, and World Vegan Day has been marked on 1 November since 1994.[16]

Earlier vegan-leaning writing includes Percy Bysshe Shelley's 1813 essay on natural diet and Asenath Nicholson's 1849 cookbook, and Frances Moore Lappé's Diet for a Small Planet (1971) sold over three million copies.[11] In 2003 two North American dietetic associations stated that well-planned vegan diets suit all life stages, and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics repeated this in later papers.[11][18] Growth in the 2010s was driven by food-industry products, social media and campaigns such as Veganuary, which drew 582,538 sign-ups in 2021.[11]

Raw veganism has a longer lineage than vegan identity itself: Wikipedia traces uncooked diets to antiquity and to early twentieth-century figures such as Maximilian Bircher-Benner, who fed patients raw food at a Swiss sanatorium from 1904, and Norman Walker in the 1970s.[19] Proponents hold that heat destroys enzymes and nutrients in food. Nutrition sources report that food enzymes play little role in human digestion and that cooking can increase availability of some nutrients such as beta-carotene.[19]

The British Dietetic Association named raw veganism among its worst celebrity diets for 2018, and sources note risks of low B12, vitamin D and energy, and low bone mass in long-term raw vegetarians.[19] In appearance forums, raw vegan eating appears in threads about skin, eye colour and general health.[12][13]

A 2021 systematic review of 48 studies in European populations found vegan diets lower in protein and associated with low intake of vitamins B2, B3, B12 and D, iodine, zinc, calcium, potassium and selenium, and no deficiency signals for vitamins A, B1, B6, C, E, iron, magnesium or folate. It reported B12 intake of 0.24-0.49 micrograms against a 2.4 microgram recommendation, and calcium below 750 mg a day in most vegans.[7]

Vitamin B12 is not reliably supplied by unfortified plant foods, so dietetic bodies advise fortified foods or supplements.[11][18] Long-chain omega-3 (EPA and DHA) is mostly absent from plant foods unless algal oil is used, and iron and zinc are less absorbable from plant sources.[18] A 2023 review of the vegan athlete says unplanned vegan diets can fall short on protein quantity and quality, iron, calcium, B12 and vitamin D.[25] A 2024 review of vegan children and adolescents found lower intake of protein, calcium and B2, lower ferritin and height, and higher B12 blood levels from supplement use, and called for better studies.[26]

A comparison of nutritional quality found differences in nutrient profiles between vegan, vegetarian, semi-vegetarian, pesco-vegetarian and omnivorous diets.[6] Modelling work has compared vegan diets with other sustainable diet strategies for health and environmental impact.[4] A 2023 review describes the components and implementation of vegan diets and their effects on adult health.[31]

Low-fat vegan diets have the most randomised evidence. In a 2006 trial in type 2 diabetes, a low-fat vegan diet improved glycaemic control and cardiovascular risk factors, and a 74-week trial in 2009 compared it with a conventional diabetes diet.[8][5] A 16-week randomised trial in overweight adults tested a low-fat vegan diet on body weight, insulin sensitivity and liver and muscle fat, and a crossover trial compared it with a Mediterranean diet.[24][27] A randomised trial of low-carbohydrate vegan diets in diabetes examined weight loss and sustainability.[28]

In a Stanford trial published in 2023, 22 pairs of identical twins followed a healthy vegan or healthy omnivorous diet for eight weeks. LDL cholesterol in the vegan group fell from 110.7 to 95.5 mg/dL against 118.5 to 116.1 in omnivores, fasting insulin dropped about 20 percent, and vegans lost about 4.2 pounds more.[22][23] The senior author noted the sample was small and baseline LDL was low.[22]

Meta-analyses of observational studies associate vegetarian and vegan diets with lower BMI, cholesterol and glucose, lower ischemic heart disease (RR 0.75) and lower total cancer incidence (RR 0.92), but not lower all-cause mortality.[1] A meta-analysis of randomised trials found weight reduction on vegetarian diets.[10] Reviews also cover vegan diets in metabolic syndrome, in rheumatoid arthritis pain and in gut microbiota composition.[30][29][3][9]
No clinical studies were found testing vegan diets for skin quality, hair, eye colour or facial appearance.

B12 deficiency can cause anaemia and neurological damage, and Wikipedia reports deficiency in up to 80 percent of vegans in some Asian countries.[11][18] Vegans may have lower bone mineral density, and a 2009 study cited on Wikipedia found vegetarian and vegan children twice as likely to be underweight.[11][18] Position papers say infants and pregnant or breastfeeding women on vegan diets need planning and supplementation, and reviews report breast milk from vegan mothers has comparable overall value with differences mainly in fatty acids and B12.[2][32]

Reviewers of The Game Changers criticised its evidence. Sports nutritionist Asker Jeukendrup wrote that it "ticks almost all the boxes of pseudoscience", while viewers credited the film with encouraging them to try plant-based eating.[20] Social-media figures promoting raw or extreme vegan diets have drawn media attention, and dietitians have cautioned about fad variants.[19]

Looksmax.org threads connect vegan diets to physique and appearance. One poster claims that consistent vegan or raw vegan eating lightened their eye colour and cites an actor's years of veganism; replies are sceptical.[12] Another thread asks whether a raw vegan diet could improve health, and responses favour animal-based eating with fruit.[13] A thread titled around a gym user's decline attributes lost gains and balding to veganism, with replies rejecting the diet.[14]

Strength-training forums such as T Nation discuss vegan protein intake; one poster cites a sports-diet book advising higher protein for vegans to cover amino acids.[33] A post on a science forum summarising a study reported men on vegan diets were perceived as less masculine, a stereotype discussed alongside masculinity-oriented diets such as carnivore.[34]

lore.intro: Vegan diets are discussed in appearance forums for skin, leanness, eye colour, hair and training, with most posters sceptical and the claims largely personal reports.[12][13][14]

claims.claim: A vegan or raw vegan diet can lighten eye colour.
claims.believers: One poster says consistent vegan eating lightened their eyes and cites an actor's long vegan period as support.[12]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined diet and iris colour change.

claims.claim: Veganism causes hair loss or loss of gym gains.
claims.believers: One thread attributes a physique decline and balding to veganism.[14]
claims.experts: Reviews note nutrients needing attention such as B12, iron and zinc and lower protein intake; trials on hair appearance were not found.[7][25]

claims.claim: Plant-based eating is healthy for skin and leanness.
claims.believers: Supporters point to leaner physiques and cleaner skin.
claims.experts: Trials show weight and cardiometabolic changes in some groups; skin outcomes are untested.[8][10][22]

claims.claim: Vegans cannot build muscle or get enough protein.
claims.believers: Strength-forum users say vegan protein needs more planning and volume to match animal sources.[33]
claims.experts: A 2023 review found vegan athletes can train without detriment if protein and micronutrients are planned, though vegan intakes are lower on average.[25][7]

claims.claim: Vegan athletes perform better because plant protein aids recovery.
claims.believers: The Game Changers features athletes crediting plant-based eating for performance and a physician arguing for faster recovery.[20]
claims.experts: The 2023 athlete review found no evidence of enhanced performance, adaptation or recovery; reviewers of the film disputed its evidence.[25][20]

claims.claim: Raw food keeps enzymes intact and is more nutritious than cooked food.
claims.believers: Raw vegans say heating destroys enzymes and nutrients.[19]
claims.experts: Sources report food enzymes play no major role in human digestion, cooking raises availability of some nutrients, and raw diets risk low B12 and low bone mass.[19]

claims.claim: Vegan diets quickly improve cardiometabolic markers.
claims.believers: Advocates cite short-term gains in cholesterol and weight.[22]
claims.experts: In the 2023 twin trial LDL cholesterol and insulin fell within eight weeks, but the trial was small and short.[22][23]

claims.claim: A vegan diet needs supplementation to be safe.
claims.believers: Vegan organisations and dietitians say B12 must come from fortified foods or supplements.[11]
claims.experts: Reviews found B12 intake far below recommendations in vegans without supplements.[7]

card.summary: Plant-only eating: good data on weight and cardiometabolic markers, nothing on looks, and B12 must be supplemented.
card.note: B12 only from fortified foods or supplements.

quick.overview:
A vegan diet excludes all animal products. In appearance circles it is discussed for skin, leanness and sometimes eye colour.

Trials in type 2 diabetes and weight loss exist; no trials examine looks.
quick.mechanism: Vegan diets are higher in fibre and lower in saturated fat and shift gut microbiota; claimed skin effects are untested.
quick.risks: Main concern is vitamin B12, plus vitamin D, calcium, iodine, iron, zinc and omega-3. Major dietetic bodies say well-planned vegan diets suit all life stages.
